records.title: The decision before the decision
records.text:
The adviser’s first responsibility
Imagine arriving in fictional Galasi. A counterpart asks you to deliver an investigation-skills course immediately. Is training already the right response?
A visible performance problem does not establish its underlying cause.
Examine the mission context, existing assistance, and counterpart capability before selecting an intervention.
Improvement begins with understanding the current, evidence-supported state.
Diagnose before prescribing.
A disciplined entry point: Observed concern; Evidence and context; Verified problem; Potential CBD response
DIAGNOSTIC DECISION PATH
A request is not a diagnosis
Select each step to follow the reasoning before committing to training.
Reported concern: What has the counterpart asked for? A request for investigation-skills training tells us what someone proposes—not why performance is weak.
Possible causes: What else might explain the problem? Consider supervision, case-file procedures, equipment, incentives and skills. These are competing hypotheses, not established facts.
Verify evidence: What would distinguish the causes? Compare records, observed practice and perspectives from the institution before making a diagnosis.
Select response: Which intervention genuinely fits? Only then consider training or another response, in line with mandate and local ownership.
First investigate the problem; then select the response. A request for training is the beginning of an inquiry—not proof that training will address the underlying capacity problem.
Imagine arriving in Galasi and hearing a familiar request: our investigators need training, and they need it quickly. It sounds reasonable. But what do we actually know? Perhaps officers lack interviewing skills. Perhaps case files are not reviewed, supervisors cannot provide guidance, or equipment is unavailable. Those are very different problems. A capacity-building adviser does not begin by choosing a course. The first professional judgement is to ask what evidence would distinguish one explanation from another. That decision protects resources, supports local ownership, and gives us a credible starting point.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Three lenses, one coherent diagnosis
records.text:
Analyses serve different purposes
Situational analysis is not a single checklist. The lesson combines three mutually informative perspectives.
Conflict analysis: what political, socioeconomic, legal, security and other dynamics shape the environment?
Response analysis: which organisations and actors are already intervening, and how?
CBD analysis: how does the counterpart actually operate, and what capacities, structures and constraints exist?
Context → existing responses → counterpart reality.
The analytical sequence: 1 · Conflict; 2 · Response; 3 · CBD
THREE COMPLEMENTARY ANALYTICAL LENSES
One situation, three questions
Explore how each analytical lens changes what you need to find out.
Conflict: What shapes the operating environment? Political, economic, social, legal, technological, environmental and security dynamics influence what is possible.
Response: Who is already engaged and doing what? Understand other actors, mandates and assistance before proposing new activities.
CBD: How does the counterpart function today? Investigate institutional performance and capacity in practice, with local participation.
There are three connected questions in this first lesson. First, what is happening in the wider conflict and operating environment? Second, who is already responding, and what are they doing? Third, how does the counterpart institution actually function? These are the conflict, response, and CBD analytical lenses. They are not competing reports. Each gives meaning to the others. A weakness inside a police unit may be influenced by insecurity outside it, by an overlapping donor programme, or by its own systems. Keep all three lenses in view before drawing a conclusion.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Establish your starting point
records.text:
Why evidence matters
Without an accurate starting point, improvement claims cannot be tested later.
Differentiate what people believe is happening from what evidence supports.
Preserve both qualitative observations and quantitative measures.
A baseline is a reference for later progress assessment—not a target or an activity list.
You cannot credibly measure change without a baseline.
From evidence to evaluation: As-is condition; CBD intervention; Later observation; Comparison
EVIDENCE TO EVALUATION
A baseline makes change observable
Follow the sequence used to make later assessment credible.
As-is baseline: What is the evidenced starting state? Document the situation before intervention, with sources, period, method and limitations.
Intervention: What change is undertaken? Record what was actually implemented. Activities do not automatically demonstrate improved capacity.
Later measurement: How will conditions be checked again? Use comparable evidence sources and clearly document any changes in method.
Comparison: Can change credibly be assessed? Compare with the baseline before making claims about outcomes or impact.
Think about how you would know, six months from now, whether an intervention actually improved performance. You need a reliable description of the situation before the intervention began. That is the baseline. It could include case-processing times, but it might also include observed procedures, documented supervision practices, or structured accounts from practitioners. A target tells us where we hope to go; the baseline tells us where we are. If those two are confused, a programme can report activity without demonstrating change. Record the source and limitations of every claim.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Structure the context with PESTEL-S
records.text:
Conflict analysis
PESTEL-S is the lesson’s organising framework for reviewing broad contextual drivers.
Political, Economic and Social factors shape incentives, institutions and trust.
Technological, Environmental and Legal factors affect service delivery and legitimate authority.
Security is the additional lens of particular importance in conflict and post-conflict settings.
Do not confuse a contextual scan with a complete conflict analysis.
Seven dimensions: Political; Economic; Social; Technological; Environmental; Legal; Security
PESTEL-S CONTEXT EXPLORER
Seven dimensions around one policing environment
Select each dimension. The questions are analytical prompts, not findings about the fictional CARANA context.
Political: Who authorises, supports or constrains reform? Consider governance, decision-making authority, incentives and commitment.
Economic: Which financial pressures affect practice? Look at resources, budgets, livelihoods and long-term sustainability.
Social: Who experiences the institution’s services? Examine trust, inclusion, expectations and community relationships.
Technological: Which systems enable or impede work? Consider information flow, equipment and the reliability of technical systems.
Environmental: What physical conditions affect service delivery? Examine relevant environmental conditions and infrastructure constraints.
Legal: What legal authorities and safeguards apply? Check powers, procedures, legal traditions and rights protections.
Security: How does insecurity change the context? Examine conflict, accessibility and constraints affecting reform.
The lesson uses PESTEL-S as a disciplined first scan of the operating context. Consider political incentives, economic pressures, social relationships, technology, the physical environment, and the legal framework. Then add security, because conflict and post-conflict settings can change what institutions are able to do from one day to the next. This is a framework for asking better questions, not a magic checklist. We are trying to understand how the environment shapes policing and reform. In an actual mission, each category should be informed by credible information and local perspectives.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Read systems, not just symptoms
records.text:
Extend the analysis
The lesson identifies additional methods for understanding conflict dynamics where the context requires them.
Actor mapping may examine power and interests as well as positions, interests and needs (PIN).
Conflict trees, escalation analysis, and needs/fears mapping explore causal relationships.
The CBD adviser need not personally complete every comprehensive analysis, but must understand its implications and seek the required expertise.
Use complementary methods when PESTEL-S alone cannot explain the situation.
Complementary methods: Actor / PIN mapping; Conflict tree; Escalation analysis; Needs and fears
CONFLICT TREE
Distinguish drivers, the presenting issue and effects
A conceptual conflict tree reveals why treating one symptom may not resolve its drivers.
Underlying drivers: What lies beneath the visible problem? Incentives, exclusion, resource disputes or institutional conditions may be contributing drivers, to be verified in the setting.
Presenting issue: What is actually happening now? Describe the current tension or operational problem without mistaking it for its cause.
Possible effects: What consequences might follow? Document observed consequences and plausible escalation pathways. Do not treat predictions as facts.
A PESTEL-S scan can tell us where to look, but sometimes we need a deeper explanation. Actor mapping can reveal who has power and who has an interest in an outcome. A position-interest-need analysis helps us distinguish what somebody says they want from what may matter underneath. Conflict trees can expose drivers and consequences, while escalation or needs-and-fears mapping can clarify dynamics. The CBD adviser does not have to conduct every specialist analysis personally. The responsibility is to recognise when the wider conflict matters, seek appropriate expertise, and integrate relevant findings into capacity-development decisions.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Law and institutional context matter
records.text:
Interpret before importing solutions
An effective reform in one jurisdiction may not transfer directly into another.
Different legal traditions affect the powers, duties and safeguards of law enforcement.
Statutory law, administrative policy and local practice must be distinguished.
Political incentives, SSR structures, culture and resources shape what changes are legitimate, feasible and sustainable.
Never assume a familiar policing model is automatically transferable.
Local-fit test: Lawful?; Contextually relevant?; Locally owned?; Feasible?
LOCAL-FIT FILTER
A good practice elsewhere is not automatically a good fit here
Explore four gates before recommending a practice from another jurisdiction.
Lawful authority: Does host-country law permit it? Check the legal powers, institutional mandate and required safeguards.
Rights and legitimacy: Does it protect affected people? Consider human rights, due process, accountability and public legitimacy.
Local ownership: Who will own the change? Engage counterpart leadership and practitioners; ensure local priorities and practical realities are understood.
Feasibility: Can it be supported and sustained? Consider budgets, staffing, organisational incentives and implementation conditions.
Imagine being asked to introduce a policing practice you know has worked elsewhere. Before recommending it, pause. Does it fit the host state's legal powers and safeguards? Does it respect local institutions and the rights of people affected? Can the counterpart sustain it? Legal systems differ, and formal rules may not describe day-to-day practice completely. We also need to understand reform structures, political incentives, culture, and resources. Good CBD is not copying a familiar solution into unfamiliar conditions. It is helping counterparts develop lawful, appropriate, and locally owned capability.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: You are not starting from zero
records.text:
Response analysis
Multiple stakeholders may already work with the same institution, sometimes pursuing different goals.
Map ongoing UN, national, bilateral and civil-society engagements relevant to the counterpart.
Identify where mandates, resources and activities complement or compete.
Avoid treating other actors automatically as obstacles—or assuming they are allies.
Know who is doing what, where and why.
Map the response landscape: Who is present?; What are they doing?; With whom?; To what end?
RESPONSE LANDSCAPE
The institution is rarely starting from zero
Explore the types of actors whose existing assistance and interests should be mapped.
National counterparts: Which host authorities are involved? Clarify institutional responsibilities, priorities and national decision-making.
UN and mission: What support already exists? Map relevant mission efforts and mandates without assuming they all operate in one way.
Bilateral and donor: What other assistance is under way? Identify programme objectives, resources, sequencing and possible overlaps.
Civil society: Who else is affected or engaged? Listen to relevant organisations and communities, respecting context and authority.
When you arrive in a mission area, you rarely find a blank slate. The host-nation institution may already be receiving support from national agencies, United Nations entities, bilateral partners, and civil society. Some activities may complement each other; others may overlap, compete, or simply ask too much of the same counterpart. Response analysis begins by mapping who is involved, what they are trying to achieve, and how their efforts interact. Avoid assuming every actor is a partner, or every disagreement is hostility. Understand the landscape first, and coordinate within your mandate.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Interests are not always visible
records.text:
Understand incentives
An actor's public position may differ from its actual interests or needs.
Power aspirations, organisational incentives and resource pressures can shape cooperation.
Host-nation reluctance to engage with external actors may be based on credible concerns.
Consider how proposed engagement may affect legitimacy, relationships and local ownership.
Understand motivations before designing engagement.
Ask beyond the formal title: Position; Interest; Need; Possible impact
POSITION · INTEREST · NEED
What is said may be only the visible layer
Reveal the three layers of a PIN analysis. They are hypotheses to explore, never assumptions about a person.
Position: What has the actor explicitly said? Record the publicly stated request or viewpoint without embellishment.
Interest: What goal might motivate that position? Explore potential priorities or incentives through respectful dialogue and evidence.
Need: What fundamental requirement may underlie it? Consider legitimate security, recognition, resources or institutional conditions. Validate rather than infer.
A stakeholder's official position is useful information, but it is not the whole story. An organisation may publicly support reform while fearing the loss of resources or influence. A counterpart may appear reluctant because previous external assistance created unrealistic promises. In other cases, there may be genuine differences in priorities. We need to explore positions, interests, needs, and possible impacts with care. This is not an invitation to manipulate people. It is a method for understanding concerns and building a respectful, credible approach to engagement and local ownership.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Coordinate to avoid unintended harm
records.text:
From mapping to responsible engagement
Even well-intended activities can duplicate work, exhaust counterparts or undermine other reforms.
Seek collaboration with relevant actors within applicable authority and mandate boundaries.
Coordinate timing, information needs and assistance where appropriate.
Record coordination risks and potential opportunities for the later SWOT analysis.
Good coordination is part of effective analysis, not an afterthought.
Risks to prevent: Duplication; Counterpart fatigue; Conflicting incentives; Wasted resources
COORDINATION AND UNINTENDED HARM
Two good programmes can still compete for one team
Examine the two programme streams, then reveal the coordination bridge.
Programme A: What is Programme A already delivering? Verify objectives, participants, schedule, dependencies and resource demands.
Programme B: Where might Programme B duplicate effort? Compare intended beneficiaries, outcomes, dates and reporting demands with existing assistance.
Coordination bridge: What changes when partners coordinate? With counterpart agreement, align needs, sequencing and information-sharing to reduce duplication and fatigue.
Good intentions can still create competing demands. Two assistance activities may appear useful individually, yet together they can duplicate effort and overload the same counterpart team.
Consider two partners arranging similar workshops for the same small police unit. Each programme might look successful on paper, yet together they take officers away from essential duties and duplicate effort. This is counterpart fatigue, and it can undermine trust. Effective coordination looks at timing, mandates, information needs, and how assistance fits with existing work. Where appropriate, advisers seek complementarity without exceeding their authority. As you map the response landscape, note opportunities for partnership and risks that may later inform SWOT and planning.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: What actually happens inside the institution?
records.text:
CBD analysis
CBD analysis looks at the counterpart's real policing systems, practice, structure and constraints.
Consider the organisation, department or unit that will own the change.
Examine performance as it occurs, rather than only what formal documents claim.
Identify issues that warrant deeper inquiry and that can later inform SWOT and baseline formulation.
Start with counterpart reality and local ownership.
Levels to investigate: Enabling environment; Organisation / department; Individual practitioner
THREE LEVELS OF CAPACITY
Performance is shaped by more than individual skills
Explore three analytical levels before attributing a weakness to staff training.
Enabling environment: Which external conditions shape the mandate? Consider legal frameworks, policy constraints, political context and wider resources.
Institution / unit: Which organisational systems affect practice? Investigate supervision, processes, accountability, staffing and logistics.
Practitioner: What can staff do in real working conditions? Examine individual competencies and behaviour, while recognising organisational constraints.
Now we move closer to the counterpart institution itself. CBD analysis asks how the organisation, department, or unit actually works. An organogram tells us something, but it cannot show whether supervision is effective or whether case files move through the system consistently. We also need to understand the enabling environment and the people carrying out the work. Local ownership matters from the beginning: the counterpart must help define the reality and the problems worth solving. Do not jump from a performance complaint to a preferred intervention before understanding the system around it.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Triangulate what you hear
records.text:
Evidence-gathering methods
One interview rarely establishes a complete operational picture.
Use suitable combinations of interviews, surveys, observation and examination of work products.
Invite counterpart self-assessment to support local participation and ownership.
Distinguish claims, direct observations and documents; examine discrepancies before concluding.
The strength of an analysis depends on the quality and diversity of evidence.
Evidence channels: Interviews; Observation; Surveys; Work products; Self-assessment
EVIDENCE TRIANGULATION
Three sources. One more defensible finding.
Select each source and see what it contributes—and what it cannot establish alone.
Interviews: What do different people report? Ask staff and supervisors about actual procedures; statements require corroboration.
Observation: What happens in practice? Observe work in context, with permission and safeguards; one visit may not be representative.
Records: What do work products show? Review file samples, registers or reports for documented practice and exceptions.
Test an account against observed practice and records. Interviews, direct observations and case documents reveal different parts of the same institutional reality; apparent inconsistencies need follow-up.
Imagine a manager telling you that every investigation is reviewed by a supervisor. That may be correct, but an evidence-based analysis checks rather than assumes. Interviews can explain intentions and experience. Observations can reveal actual practice. Surveys, work products, records, and counterpart self-assessment can add different perspectives. When these sources disagree, the difference itself deserves investigation. This is triangulation: not simply collecting more information, but comparing kinds of evidence to reach a more defensible understanding. Always consider access, reliability, consent, and appropriate handling of sensitive information.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Map people, power and interest
records.text:
Stakeholder analysis
Stakeholders are those involved in, influencing or affected by proposed CBD activities.
Identify both formal decision-makers and actors with informal influence.
Assess their level of interest, influence and potential impact.
Choose engagement and communication approaches proportionate to their role and revisable over time.
Influence and interest guide engagement, not simplistic labels of good and bad actors.
Power / interest planning: High power · high interest; High power · lower interest; Lower power · high interest; Lower power · lower interest
POWER / INTEREST MATRIX
Choose engagement proportionate to power and interest
The horizontal axis is interest; the vertical axis is influence. Explore each quadrant.
High influence · lower interest: Maintain appropriate engagement Monitor key decisions, understand barriers and consult when necessary.
High influence · high interest: Engage closely Involve relevant decision-makers appropriately and revisit changing positions.
Lower influence · lower interest: Monitor and keep access open Do not dismiss perspectives or assume influence and interest are fixed.
Lower influence · high interest: Listen and involve Affected groups may have essential information despite limited formal influence.
An organisational chart identifies formal authority, but reform can also be shaped by informal influence. Stakeholder analysis helps us identify who will be affected, who can influence the process, and who needs meaningful participation. Interest and influence may change over time. A powerful decision-maker with little day-to-day interest may require a different approach from practitioners who are deeply affected but have limited formal authority. These are planning considerations, not labels of good and bad people. Return to the map as relationships, needs, and expectations change.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Five areas of institutional capacity
records.text:
The areas axis
The lesson identifies five broad areas in which national police capacity should be assessed.
Police services: knowledge, skills, command and control.
Enabling services: people, training, finance, logistics and support.
Police policy formulation; accountability mechanisms; and stakeholder engagement.
A weakness in investigation outcomes can originate well beyond an investigator's skills.
Five CBD areas: Police services; Enabling services; Police policy formulation; Accountability mechanisms; Stakeholder engagement
FIVE CBD CAPACITY AREAS
Institutional capacity has five connected areas
Explore each area before deciding where a verified issue belongs.
Police services: How well are core policing services delivered? Consider professional policing practice, command and control and actual service performance.
Enabling services: Which support systems enable delivery? Investigate staffing, training systems, finance, logistics and other administrative support.
Police policy formulation: How is institutional policy developed? Examine how rules and guidance are formulated and maintained.
Accountability mechanisms: How is conduct and performance reviewed? Consider responsibility, internal review, oversight and answerability.
Stakeholder engagement: How does the institution engage others? Examine working relationships, participation and relevant external interaction.
A complaint about weak investigations could lead us to focus immediately on investigators' skills. The CBD analysis framework asks us to look wider. Police services are one area, but enabling services, policy formulation, accountability mechanisms, and stakeholder engagement also matter. Perhaps the problem is related to personnel management, guidance, oversight, logistics, or communication with communities. Using the five areas prevents us from treating every symptom as an individual training gap. Each finding should be based on evidence from the counterpart and the operating context.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Six dimensions cross every area
records.text:
The dimensions axis
The same institutional issue may have consequences across several cross-cutting requirements.
Policing practice, environmental sustainability and conflict prevention.
Human rights, gender and comprehensive protection of civilians (CPOC).
Human rights and protection considerations are substantive analytical obligations, not decoration.
The five areas × six dimensions provide a disciplined classification framework.
Six cross-cutting dimensions: Policing practice; Environmental sustainability; Conflict prevention; Human rights; Gender; CPOC
The second part of the CBD matrix is the set of six cross-cutting dimensions. These include policing practice, environmental sustainability, conflict prevention, human rights, gender, and comprehensive protection of civilians. They are not a separate box to tick at the end. Each dimension asks us to examine how a capacity issue affects the way policing is delivered and experienced. For example, a new reporting process may improve efficiency while also raising questions about access, accountability, or protection. The five areas and six dimensions work together to structure that analysis.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Move from observations to structured issues
records.text:
The 5 × 6 analytical matrix
The goal is to connect source-based institutional issues with the relevant area and dimension.
Read each evidence item and identify the underlying capacity or institutional issue.
Choose the most relevant CBD area and specialised dimension; justify the link.
Avoid automatically assigning everything to general policing practice when a more specific dimension applies.
A useful matrix records defensible issues—not a list of unsupported assumptions.
Classification logic: Evidence item; CBD area; Relevant dimension; Issue to investigate
Now imagine an observation that an institution has no dependable system for tracking equipment maintenance. Where does that issue belong in the CBD matrix? Start with the evidence, identify the institutional issue, and then justify the most relevant area and cross-cutting dimension. The purpose is not to fill every cell. The purpose is to place credible findings where they help the team understand needs and design a responsible response. Avoid turning assumptions into findings, and resist placing everything under general policing practice when another dimension is more informative.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: From findings to SWOT
records.text:
Structured synthesis
Once the CBD analysis identifies issues, appraise them as strengths, weaknesses, opportunities or threats relevant to the proposed change.
Strengths and weaknesses examine factors internal to the relevant counterpart or system.
Opportunities and threats examine consequential external conditions or influences.
Ground each entry in earlier analysis; avoid invented or generic entries.
SWOT must be evidence-led and should follow—rather than substitute for—analysis.
SWOT lens: Strengths · internal; Weaknesses · internal; Opportunities · external; Threats · external
SWOT becomes useful after we understand the context, responses, and counterpart institution. Strengths and weaknesses describe relevant internal factors. Opportunities and threats concern external conditions that could enable or obstruct progress. The distinction sounds straightforward, but an unsupported SWOT is little more than opinion. Trace each entry back to analysis and evidence. Be clear about the institution and level being examined. A strong internal practice might create an entry point for improvement, while an external risk may need to be addressed during later planning. SWOT summarises findings; it does not replace the analysis.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: Record an evaluable as-is baseline
records.text:
Bridge to later CBD phases
The baseline fixes the current situation before interventions and targets are established.
Quantitative indicators can include verified counts, rates, proportions or elapsed time.
Qualitative indicators can include documented practices, observed conditions and structured narratives.
Record data sources, reporting periods, limitations and later verification methods wherever possible.
An as-is baseline can later be compared with a defined to-be state.
Baseline example · illustrative only: Issue: inconsistent case tracking; As-is: no verified central register; Evidence: file review + interviews; Later measure: adoption and use
AS-IS BASELINE ≠ FUTURE TARGET
Keep observed reality separate from desired results
The illustration uses invented teaching numbers, not actual CARANA findings.
As-is evidence: What was verified before change? Illustrative only: 12 of 40 sampled files recorded a supervisory review in a specified period. The baseline is a measured starting point, with stated limitations.
Desired future: What would an agreed result look like? A target is set through later planning. It must not be substituted for observed baseline evidence.
Comparable measure: Can the same indicator be tracked later? Document the sampling frame, reporting period, definitions and verification method so outcomes can be compared.
A baseline is our evidence-supported description of the current state. It might contain verified counts, proportions, or elapsed times. It can also describe current procedures, supervision practices, or observed conditions. What matters is that another adviser could understand what was measured, when, how, and with what limitations. Later, that record can be compared with a defined desired state to examine change. Avoid writing a target as though it were a baseline, or presenting a guessed number as verified. Careful baseline design makes future evaluation credible.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training on Capacity-Building and Development, Lesson 1 (2021; PDF dated 07/2023)

records.title: You are ready for the CARANA workbench
records.text:
Apply the complete sequence
In the existing CARANA activity, investigate the fictional Galasi Criminal Investigations Services using the lesson's analytical tools.
Review the scenario and stakeholder context before proposing solutions.
Build a structured picture using the areas–dimensions matrix, SWOT and an as-is baseline.
Use the findings to identify credible entry points for the next CBD phase.
Pass the final checkpoint to continue to the guided practice step.
Carry your learning into practice: Context; Actors; Institution; SWOT + baseline; Exercise
YOUR NEXT STEP IS AN EVIDENCE-LED WORKBENCH
Carry findings into the CARANA activity
Explore the handover from analysis to practical planning. The example does not disclose exercise answers.
Context: What broader conditions matter? Bring forward verified conflict-environment observations.
Responses: Who is already involved? Map actors, objectives, overlaps, stakeholder interest and influence.
Institution: What does the counterpart do? Document capacity issues across relevant areas and dimensions.
Synthesis: What findings are defensible? Ground SWOT and an as-is baseline in the available evidence.
Workbench: How will you practise? Apply the analytical tools to the fictional CARANA exercise before selecting future objectives.
You have now followed the analytical sequence from the operating environment to a structured picture of the counterpart. In the original CARANA workbench, you will examine the scenario, identify relevant actors, build an area-and-dimension analysis, and draw together evidence for SWOT and the baseline. This is where the lesson becomes practical. Take your time with the information. Distinguish source facts from assumptions, justify the issues you record, and resist jumping to solutions. Your objective is a credible diagnosis that can support the next phase of Capacity Building and Development.
