records.lessonTitle: Objective Setting, Prioritisation and Performance Framework
records.title: A police objective sits within a larger system
records.text:
An investigation reform can fail if it improves police output while overwhelming the next part of the justice system.
Start with the authorised mission mandate, the host-State capacity-building framework and the national security framework.
The 2023 lesson links this alignment to UNSCR 2151, SDG 16, the SGF UN Police policy and CBD guidelines. These references connect peace, rule of law, inclusive and accountable institutions, and police development; they are historical teaching references, not a statement that mission guidance is unchanged.
Consider security providers and governance or oversight actors, including State and non-State stakeholders. A counterpart’s concern may reveal a missing dependency.
Alignment requires considering how reform affects the wider justice and oversight system.
A request to strengthen police investigations can sound like a self-contained technical task. In practice, more cases may also affect prosecutors, courts, detention and oversight. Start by asking what change is authorised and how it fits the host-State framework. The lesson places police development within the wider security-sector architecture. That connection is not paperwork added after choosing an activity; it can change the objective itself. Use the map to consider each relationship, then decide which dependency would need discussion. You are testing the coherence of a proposed change, not choosing an institutional reform on someone else’s behalf.
How police capacity shifts affect the wider justice system
Mandate: Establish what support is authorised.
National framework: Discuss how the intended result supports nationally determined priorities.
Justice relationships: Check implications for prosecution, courts, corrections and oversight.
Consult the applicable mission mandate and current institutional guidance when applying the historical source.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 2 — Objective Setting (July 2023)

records.lessonTitle: Objective Setting, Prioritisation and Performance Framework
records.title: Ownership is maintained through participation
records.text:
A signature on a project document is useful evidence of agreement, but it does not by itself establish enduring ownership.
Invite counterparts into analysis and objective setting, then maintain dialogue as conditions change.
Document agreements and connect CBD priorities with counterpart priorities without treating consultation as a substitute for rights and mandate obligations.
Sustainability includes affordability, capability, relevance, the enabling environment and continued commitment. Reform can shift power and privileges; acknowledge concerns respectfully.
Ownership needs continuing engagement and cannot be inferred once for the entire programme.
Imagine that the original counterpart champion leaves midway through an initiative. A signed agreement still exists, yet participation becomes uncertain. It would be easy to call this resistance and carry on. A more useful response is to explore what has changed: responsibilities, resources, incentives or the interpretation of the objective. Ownership is maintained through participation, dialogue and documented agreements. It also involves the people affected by the change, not only the person who signs. Consider whether the process could continue without the adviser’s daily encouragement. That question connects ownership with sustainability and may reveal a decision that needs to be revisited.
External blueprint vs counterpart-owned diagnosis
Participation: Ask who helps define the problem and intended result.
Agreement: Record responsibilities and the reasoning behind priorities.
Review: Reconfirm ownership when leaders, incentives or resources change.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 2 — Objective Setting (July 2023)

records.lessonTitle: Objective Setting, Prioritisation and Performance Framework
records.title: Make trade-offs visible
records.text:
More reform needs may exist than available time, people or funding can address.
Compare alternatives consistently rather than selecting the most visible request.
The lesson suggests beneficiary importance, strategic importance, complementarity and implementability as comparison lenses.
Record reasoning and assumptions so choices are transparent and defensible. Revisit priorities when evidence changes, while avoiding endless review that prevents action.
A scoring aid supports judgement; it cannot remove the need to understand prerequisites.
Two proposals can both be worthwhile while only one can be supported now. A comparison method makes your reasoning visible, but the method contains choices of its own. Which perspectives count, how strongly are they weighted, and what information supports each rating? Try changing the weights in the invented comparison. A different ranking should prompt discussion rather than surprise. Then look beyond the total: a dependency may require foundational work first. The official participant chart is more detailed than this illustration. Use this exercise to understand judgement under constraints before applying the actual chart to your own analytical findings.
Weighting priorities without concealing hard constraints
Beneficiary value: Whose safety or service experience improves?
Strategic fit: How does the proposal support agreed reform aims?
Complementarity: Does it reinforce other initiatives or depend on them?
Implementability: Can it be carried out with the relevant capacity and resources?

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 2 — Objective Setting (July 2023)

records.lessonTitle: Objective Setting, Prioritisation and Performance Framework
records.title: Turn an intention into a testable objective
records.text:
“Improve investigations” names a worthwhile direction but leaves the expected change unclear.
Specify the change and who or what it concerns. Make progress measurable and time-bound.
Check achievability with those responsible and relevance to the diagnosed need and strategic framework.
Agree a realistic scope before selecting the exact target. A numerical target invented without baseline evidence is not a sound objective.
SMART wording should make an agreed and feasible result testable; it should not disguise missing evidence.
SMART is most useful as a conversation about meaning and feasibility. If an objective says that a process will improve, ask what change would be visible, who is responsible, and when it could reasonably be reviewed. Do not fill a gap in baseline evidence with a confident-looking percentage. Record what is known and what still needs agreement. The drafting scaffold asks you to separate these decisions so that a counterpart can challenge them. It will check only whether you have written something, not whether your professional judgement is sound. Take the revised objective into the practical workbench for further scrutiny.
Five test questions that turn intent into a SMART objective
Specific: Define the intended change and scope.
Measurable: Specify how progress can be observed.
Achievable and relevant: Check capability, constraints and connection to the diagnosed need.
Time-bound: State when the result will be reviewed.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 2 — Objective Setting (July 2023)

records.lessonTitle: Objective Setting, Prioritisation and Performance Framework
records.title: Test the objective in a counterpart briefing
records.text:
A clear-looking objective can still hide different assumptions about whose service should improve.
Read the result from the counterpart’s perspective: who is responsible and who experiences the change?
Explain the intended change in plain language before agreeing the number. A target without a shared definition can create misleading agreement.
Invite a challenge about capability, inclusion and continuing support. Document the decision and its unresolved assumptions.
Shared wording is useful only when the parties share its operational meaning.
Picture a briefing where everyone agrees to improve case handling. One person means faster processing; another means more complete documentation. A shared phrase has hidden two different intentions. Before choosing a target, invite the counterpart to describe what successful practice would look like and who would maintain it. Then check whether the measure captures that intention. You may need several perspectives, but not an unlimited number of indicators. A useful objective makes discussion more precise. It does not eliminate disagreement by sounding technical. The example is invented and does not supply the CARANA activity’s priorities.
Reading beneath polite surface agreement in a counterpart briefing
Proposed result: Identify the service change, not just the event.
Counterpart interpretation: Check who will act and how the change fits existing responsibilities.
Agreed revision: Record scope, evidence and remaining decisions.
Initial proposal: Conduct a file-review workshop by June. (This specifies delivery and a date but does not define the change in practice.)
More defensible approach: Agree a defined review routine and evidence of its use in the selected unit, with a feasible target and review date established from the baseline. (This links the activity to a result and exposes what must still be agreed. It is a structure for discussion, not a completed SMART objective.)

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 2 — Objective Setting (July 2023)

records.lessonTitle: Objective Setting, Prioritisation and Performance Framework
records.title: Choose indicators that inform decisions
records.text:
The number of delivered workshops may be easy to count without telling you whether policing practice improved.
Choose measures that reflect the intended result and can be gathered and managed.
The source emphasises countable indicators while allowing more than one perspective on a complex objective.
Specify the observation and compare it with the baseline and intended result. Keep the number of indicators proportionate to the collection effort.
An activity count does not establish the quality of the intended result.
A workshop register answers a delivery question. A review of work products may answer a practice question. Neither automatically explains why a change occurred. Begin with the intended result and ask what evidence would be useful for the next decision. You may need more than one perspective, but each measure creates work for someone. Choose a manageable set, define the observations and explain their limits. In the classification exercise, distinguish a delivered activity from evidence about practice and from a weakness in the evidence. The aim is not to reject numbers; it is to make them meaningful.
What an output count shows vs what stays unmeasured
Result: What change does the objective seek?
Indicator: What observation would suggest progress?
Collection: Who can obtain comparable evidence and how?
Use: What decision would this evidence inform?

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 2 — Objective Setting (July 2023)

records.lessonTitle: Objective Setting, Prioritisation and Performance Framework
records.title: A stronger number needs a defensible method
records.text:
An indicator is only as useful as the observation and comparison behind it.
State what is counted and the relevant population or denominator. Keep the definition stable across observations.
Plan a feasible evidence source, collection responsibility and review schedule. Consider missing records and whose experience may be absent.
Use the indicator to support a decision. Explain uncertainty rather than treating a favourable number as proof that the intervention caused the change.
A repeatable measurement plan turns a number into evidence that can be questioned.
Suppose a report says that review quality improved from half of files to four fifths. Before celebrating, ask whether the same definition was used, whether the files came from comparable work and how they were selected. Perhaps the second sample contained only simpler files. That does not make measurement useless; it tells you what to investigate before drawing a conclusion. The lesson links indicators with later evaluation. Keep the collection burden proportionate, but make the method understandable enough for another adviser to repeat. The figures in this example are invented and are not findings from CARANA.
Why denominators and sampling rules determine whether numbers mislead
Definition: What exactly is observed and what does the number refer to?
Collection: How, when and by whom will comparable evidence be obtained?
Interpretation: What decision is supported, and which alternative explanation remains?

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 2 — Objective Setting (July 2023)

records.lessonTitle: Objective Setting, Prioritisation and Performance Framework
records.title: Carry defensible choices into practice
records.text:
Your analytical findings now need to become a manageable set of justified objectives.
Use your own Lesson 1 findings to identify candidate objectives, then compare their importance and feasibility.
The official group task identifies 6–10 candidate objectives, uses the participant comparison chart while leaving its risk category aside at this stage, then phrases the top two objectives using SMART. The chart also considers donor interest; the four preceding teaching lenses are a concise introduction, not the complete chart.
Prepare to explain why a choice is prioritised, which prerequisite matters and how its result could be measured.
Planning needs a reasoned objective rather than a ranked list alone.
Your Lesson 1 findings are the starting point for the official objective-setting activity. The task is not to recover a hidden ideal list. Identify six to ten candidate objectives, compare them using the participant chart while leaving its risk category aside at this stage, and phrase the top two using SMART. Keep the distinction between that chart and our simpler teaching comparison clear. Before moving to planning, explain why your choices matter, which dependencies affect their sequence and how progress could be observed. Another participant may make a defensible different choice. The discussion of evidence and assumptions is part of the learning.
Preparing evidence and questions for the Module 2 workbench
Evidence: Carry forward your own diagnosis.
Priorities: Explain trade-offs and dependencies.
Objectives: Make the selected result testable.
Reflection: Ask a peer what could invalidate your reasoning.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 2 — Objective Setting (July 2023)

records.title: Begin with the result, then test the chain
records.text:
A familiar activity is not a sufficient starting point for a reform plan.
Work from the agreed goal and outcomes toward the outputs and activities needed to support them.
For each intended result, a logframe row states the result, how it will be measured or verified, where evidence will come from, and the external factors or assumptions that could prevent achievement. The reveal below explains the result hierarchy; construct the four-column plan in the linked workbench.
After designing from the intended result, check the chain upward: can the inputs and activities plausibly deliver outputs that support the outcome?
Goals should guide the required activities; a bottom-up check then tests their plausibility.
Begin with the change that the agreed objective seeks. Familiar activities are easier to describe, but choosing them first can make the plan serve the activity rather than the result. Work downward from the goal and outcomes, then check upward whether the activities and inputs can support the chain. This is not a guarantee of causation. It is a way to expose what needs to be true and what evidence could challenge the plan. In the next practice row, test the horizontal connection as well: a result needs a relevant measure, a credible evidence source and explicit external conditions.
Tracing backward from the intended outcome to inputs
Goal: State the wider intent.
Outcome: Describe the change the intervention seeks to support.
Output: Identify what the activity will directly deliver.
Activity and input: Plan the work and resources needed.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 3 — Planning Activities (July 2023)

records.title: Check one logframe row across four columns
records.text:
A result, its measure, its evidence source and its assumptions must refer to the same intended change.
Describe a result at a clear level: do not call a delivered session an institutional outcome.
Choose a measure that speaks to that result, then identify where credible evidence can be obtained.
Make external conditions explicit. Test the row horizontally as well as the result chain vertically.
A coherent row asks one connected result-and-evidence question.
A logframe can look complete when every cell contains words, yet the row may not make sense. Suppose the result concerns the use of a review routine, the indicator counts delivered workshops and the evidence source is a procurement register. Each cell sounds measurable, but they do not address the same result. Read the row across and ask what the evidence would actually tell you. Then read the hierarchy to see how this result contributes to the next level. The scaffold supports a single row for an invented example. It does not complete the official exercise or establish that your proposed reform is feasible.
Horizontal logic across the four logical-framework columns
Result: What change or direct deliverable is this row about?
Verification measure: What observation addresses that result?
Evidence source: How will that observation be obtained?
External condition: What necessary condition is outside this activity’s direct control?

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 3 — Planning Activities (July 2023)

records.title: Explain the missing middle
records.text:
A theory of change asks how and why an activity is expected to contribute to change in its context.
State the expected change before listing actions.
Explain the causal reasoning: if the action occurs, what should follow, and why?
Identify assumptions about people, institutions and politics that could break the connection. This reasoning should influence the plan rather than become a separate diagram.
Outputs need a plausible mechanism and conditions to contribute to an outcome.
A theory of change makes a professional claim open to scrutiny. If we support this action, what change is expected, and why should it follow in this setting? The word because matters. It identifies the mechanism rather than simply connecting boxes with arrows. Now ask what could prevent the mechanism from working: incentives, authority, time or another institutional dependency. Some conditions may be influenced by the programme and others may need to be monitored. Use the classification exercise to separate what is delivered from what should change and what remains an assumption. That distinction helps improve the plan before implementation.
Testing the causal bridge inside your Theory of Change
If: Name the action or condition.
Then: Describe the expected change.
Because: Explain the mechanism and evidence behind it.
Provided that: Surface assumptions that require checking.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 3 — Planning Activities (July 2023)

records.title: Budget for results
records.text:
Resource planning should follow the results a programme seeks, rather than repeat last year’s list of activities.
The lesson introduces results-based budgeting as linking objectives and expected results to resource requirements and performance measures.
Check whether the required people, time, tools and recurrent support are affordable and coherent with the logframe.
Make trade-offs explicit: adding a resource is justified by its contribution to a result, not merely by its availability.
Results-oriented resource planning must consider what is needed to sustain the intended capability.
A budget can be internally accurate yet poorly connected to the objective. Consider a plan that funds a useful tool but leaves out the people or support required to use it. The resource list may be affordable while the result remains infeasible. The lesson introduces results-based budgeting as deriving resource requirements from predefined objectives and expected results, then connecting performance with measures. Use that logic to challenge a resource request. Which result does it support, what continuing requirement accompanies it, and what trade-off is being made? This is instructional reasoning about a plan, not an approved UN budget or funding decision.
Matching resource lines to each planned operational step
Expected result: Clarify the result being resourced.
Requirements: Derive resources from the planned route to that result.
Performance: Use indicators to assess progress.
Revision: Review assumptions when costs or conditions change.
Initial proposal: Purchase the available equipment and schedule the same activities as last year. (This starts with resources and familiar actions rather than the result being sought.)
More defensible approach: Derive people, equipment, support and continuing requirements from the agreed result, then use performance measures to review delivery and progress. (Results-based budgeting connects strategic intent, resource choices and measurement; the example is not an approved budget.)

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 3 — Planning Activities (July 2023)

records.title: Census and vetting require a distinct mandate
records.text:
Identifying the personnel body and assessing eligibility are sensitive institutional processes, not general substitutes for training or supervision.
Census and vetting define the relevant personnel body and eligibility under the applicable criteria.
National ownership, law, due process, individual rights, risk management and relevant expertise are essential to the source’s treatment.
A mandate determines the adviser’s role. Vetting does not replace criminal prosecution of human-rights violations. This teaching overview does not qualify a learner to conduct the process.
Choose tools for the verified problem and the required expertise, safeguards and implementation conditions.
Imagine an institution wants to address serious concerns about personnel eligibility. That is a different task from improving a team’s daily competence. The lesson treats census and vetting as professional tools with significant conditions: national ownership, a legal basis, due process, individual rights and proper risk management. The mission mandate also affects whether an adviser supports or leads a process. Do not turn these safeguards into a short checklist that appears to authorise a programme. Identify the relevant authority and expertise before proceeding. The distinction matters because using a powerful tool for the wrong problem can damage both people and the reform process.
Separating UNPOL technical advice from sovereign host-State mandates
Personnel question: Identify the actual eligibility or personnel-body question.
Authority and safeguards: Establish applicable mandate, law, national ownership, rights and due process.
Professional implementation: Identify competent actors and risks; an instructional overview is not authorisation.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 3 — Planning Activities (July 2023)

records.title: Match training and MMA to the diagnosed need
records.text:
Different support needs can coexist within the same unit; one activity may not address them all.
Training helps close a competence gap when learning conditions, audience needs and motivation support it.
Monitoring develops an informed picture of practice. Advising supports situational assistance; mentoring supports personal development.
MMA needs subject expertise and interpersonal skills, with awareness of the adviser’s limits. The source highlights co-location as an especially effective setting.
Specify the support need before naming the activity.
An officer may understand a procedure yet need help applying it to a difficult situation. Another may need to learn a skill, while a supervisor may benefit from a longer developmental relationship. These are related but different needs. The lesson presents training and MMA as tools that should be selected with care, not as interchangeable programme labels. Think about both the recipient’s needs and your own professional limits. A co-located setting may support continuing contact, but proximity alone does not provide expertise or trust. Use the distinctions to justify a support choice before planning its details.
Selecting training vs MMA around the actual capability bottleneck
Competence gap: Ask what a person needs to learn and whether training can address it.
Situational support: Consider advice for a specific decision or practice challenge.
Development relationship: Consider mentoring and continuing observation of how practice develops.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 3 — Planning Activities (July 2023)

records.title: A new policy needs a route into practice
records.text:
Issuing a standard can establish direction without ensuring that anyone can apply it.
Policy development can introduce coherent standards and contribute to reform direction.
Connect appropriate legislative and policy work with dissemination, explanation, training or advice where needed.
Monitor implementation and compliance. A published document is an output, not proof that practice conforms to it.
Plan for the use of a standard, not just its publication.
Picture a carefully written procedure sitting on a shelf while staff continue their old routine. The document may be sound, yet its implementation is incomplete. The lesson connects policy work with further actions such as communication, training, advice and compliance monitoring. Ask what changes for the person who must use the policy and how that person will obtain support. Then plan what observation would show use or reveal a difficulty. This is the same results logic used in a logframe: a useful output contributes through a mechanism, not through its existence alone. The situation is invented, not a CARANA solution.
How a signed policy moves or stalls between headquarters and desks
Standard: Clarify the intended practice and the applicable authority.
Implementation support: Enable people to understand and apply the standard.
Observed use: Check practice and feed findings back into support.
Initial proposal: Publish a new review procedure. (This states a deliverable without describing how staff will apply it.)
More defensible approach: Explain the procedure with responsible counterparts, provide needed application support, and examine evidence of its use. (This links the output to practice while keeping implementation assumptions open to review.)

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 3 — Planning Activities (July 2023)

records.title: Distinguish momentum from structural reform
records.text:
A small community project may build confidence while leaving deeper institutional constraints unresolved.
The source presents quick impact projects as small-scale, low-cost and short-duration confidence-building tools.
Connect an incentive to a verified community need and a responsible implementation arrangement. Do not claim a short project establishes lasting reform.
The lesson discusses trust funds as possible support; availability and eligibility need current verification rather than assumptions about funding access.
A useful incentive can create momentum without establishing long-term institutional change.
A small project may help demonstrate responsiveness and build confidence. It should not be asked to prove a deeper institutional transformation that it was never designed to achieve. The lesson presents quick impact projects within this limited purpose and discusses trust funds as potential support. Keep both the opportunity and the limits visible. Begin with a community need, check the implementation arrangement and ask what would show the immediate output. Then distinguish that from the longer change the CBD process seeks. Funding availability must be established through the relevant current arrangements; a teaching reference does not establish eligibility or a commitment.
Activity volume vs structural institutional change
Need: What locally expressed need does the project address?
Confidence: How might it support trust in the process?
Limits: What institutional change remains outside its scope?
Resources: What authorised funding and implementation arrangements are actually available?

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 3 — Planning Activities (July 2023)

records.title: Make risks actionable
records.text:
A list of threats is useful only if it informs decisions and responsibilities.
Identify risks with counterparts, then analyse likelihood and impact.
Evaluate which risks need a response and record mitigation or preventive actions in a risk log.
Assign review responsibilities and revisit the log as conditions change. A high score alone does not specify the action required.
Risk management requires a response and continuing review, not just classification.
When a risk is identified, it is tempting to focus on its colour or score. The useful question is what the judgement changes. Consider likelihood and consequence separately, then decide what can prevent the event, reduce its effect or provide an alternative if it occurs. In the matrix, a low likelihood does not erase a severe consequence. The illustrative product is a discussion aid, not an authorised threshold. Your risk log also needs responsibility and review. Explain who will notice changed conditions and who can act. This converts uncertainty into an operational conversation rather than a list of warnings.
Separating probability, consequence, and response strategy
Identify: Describe a possible event and how it affects the objective.
Analyse and rank: Consider likelihood and consequences.
Respond: Choose prevention, mitigation or a contingency response.
Monitor: Track changes and whether the response is working.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 3 — Planning Activities (July 2023)

records.title: Prepare an alternative path before disruption
records.text:
A contingency plan prepares for an outcome that differs from the expected course.
Identify and prioritise disruption scenarios, then plan how essential activity can continue or recover.
Specify key people, resources and responsibilities; share the plan with those who may need to act.
Keep it current. Use your own Lesson 2 objective to construct a logframe and risk analysis in the original workbench, then seek a peer’s challenge to your assumptions.
A contingency plan must be understood, assigned and maintained to be usable.
A contingency plan is useful when people can recognise its trigger and carry out their responsibilities. Imagine the original venue becomes unavailable. Repeating the timetable in a document does not identify what should happen next. Decide what essential function must continue, who can choose an alternative and which resources or safeguards are necessary. Share the arrangement with the people affected and check that it remains current. The same reasoning belongs in the practical planning work, alongside your logframe and risk analysis. A colleague should be able to question the response without needing to guess what its author intended.
Linking early disruption signals to pre-agreed fallback paths
Trigger: What event requires the alternative response?
Continuity: Which functions and resources need protecting?
Responsibility: Who decides, acts and communicates?
Review: When will the alternative plan be checked?

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 3 — Planning Activities (July 2023)

records.title: A sound plan still needs a local fit
records.text:
A plan is an informed starting point. Its implementation must respond to the organisation and communities it affects.
Examine how organisational culture shapes routines and behaviour before importing a familiar practice.
Develop responses with host-State police and relevant stakeholders so they address local problems.
Consider how culture, gender, ethnicity and religion affect policing relationships and who benefits.
Keep the context under review as implementation progresses.
Implementation begins with understanding how a proposed change will work here.
Imagine introducing a case-review routine that worked well in your own police service. The document may be sound, but the way authority, trust and daily work operate in another institution can be different. Ask counterparts how the routine would affect their responsibilities and the people they serve. Consider whose concerns have not yet been heard, including different experiences of women and men. The lesson asks advisers to develop local solutions with stakeholders. That requires listening to organisational practice rather than assuming a translated procedure will be adopted. The example is invented; it is a prompt for inquiry, not a finding about CARANA.
Headquarters design assumptions vs daily station realities
Proposed change: Identify the purpose of the practice and the capacity gap it is intended to address.
Local practice: Explore routines, organisational culture and constraints through counterpart dialogue.
Different experiences: Check how the change may affect groups differently, including gender and community relationships.
Joint adaptation: Agree a locally relevant response and monitor how it operates.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 4 — Implementation (July 2023)

records.title: Communicate for understanding and participation
records.text:
The same reform message may need different explanations for leadership, supervisors and operational counterparts.
Match the message to the stakeholder’s role and context while keeping the facts consistent.
Use the seven Cs: clarity, correctness, completeness, conciseness, concreteness, coherence and courtesy.
Check understanding through dialogue instead of assuming that delivering a message secures agreement.
Use respectful language that explains the issue without labelling counterparts as the problem.
Clear communication connects accurate information with the people who need to act.
Imagine explaining a new reporting routine to a commander and to officers who must use it during a busy shift. The purpose is the same, but each audience needs different operational detail. A clear message tells people what is changing and why. Correctness and completeness keep it factual and sufficient. Conciseness, concreteness and coherence make it usable. Courtesy keeps the discussion respectful. These seven communication principles work together; brevity should not remove information needed to act safely. Ask a counterpart to describe what the change would mean in practice. This short exchange can reveal confusion that a formal announcement would miss.
Four communication checks before launching an implementation step
Know the audience: Choose the level and practical detail appropriate to the role, position and context.
Build a usable message: Combine the seven Cs so the explanation is factual, sufficient, logical and respectful.
Check understanding: Invite questions and listen to how the counterpart interprets the proposed action.
Adjust the explanation: Clarify the message while preserving its facts and purpose.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 4 — Implementation (July 2023)

records.section: Support change as well as delivery
records.title: A delivered activity is not sustained change
records.text:
Completing the work plan does not automatically prepare people to adopt and sustain new practices.
CBD builds and retains capability; change management prepares, guides and supports those affected.
Consider executive support, active sponsorship, communication, ownership, resources and culture.
Expect adoption and sustainment to take time beyond introducing the solution.
Investigate combinations of constraints rather than blaming one individual for every setback.
Manage the human and institutional change alongside the CBD activities.
Imagine a unit receives a useful tool and completes the planned training. Weeks later, daily routines have barely changed. This does not by itself tell you that staff cannot learn. The lesson distinguishes building capability from guiding the change that allows it to be used. Leadership may not support the new routine, responsibilities may be unclear, or people may not see themselves as owners of the change. Several constraints can operate together. Discuss the drivers and barriers with counterparts, and consider how support will continue after the initial activity. Adoption and sustainment are longer-term objectives, not automatic consequences of delivering a workshop or distributing equipment.
Tracking delivered workshops alongside changed institutional habits
Capability: People and institutions obtain, improve and retain the resources needed to perform.
Readiness and support: Prepare people for the change and provide guidance during adoption.
Ownership and leadership: Identify active support, meaningful counterpart participation and institutional commitment.
Sustainment: Monitor whether the changed practice continues in everyday work.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 4 — Implementation (July 2023)

records.section: Support change as well as delivery
records.title: Monitor implementation and respond early
records.text:
Implementation is an ongoing responsibility. It requires checking progress and scanning the environment.
Review implementation periodically instead of treating activities as set and forget.
Watch for resistance, timing problems, weak support and unintended consequences.
Use monitoring to identify when direction, activities or objectives may need review.
Distinguish routine progress checks from the deeper outcome and impact assessment addressed in evaluation.
Notice emerging constraints early enough to act with counterparts.
Imagine that a planned activity is progressing on schedule while participation by a key group is falling. A completion calendar alone would miss this signal. The lesson calls for systematic review and environmental scanning throughout implementation. Check what is progressing, what is changing and what unintended effects may be emerging. Monitoring can highlight the need to revisit activities or objectives, but it should not be presented as a full assessment of outcomes or impact. Discuss the signal and its possible causes with counterparts. Responsible resilience means remaining engaged and adapting to evidence; it does not mean continuing an ineffective approach simply because the original plan was approved.
Early implementation signals vs end-of-cycle surprises
Progress check: Examine delivery and implementation against the agreed plan.
Context scan: Look for changing support, participation, constraints and opportunities.
Joint interpretation: Distinguish an observed signal from an assumed explanation.
Review and action: Agree what needs attention and continue monitoring the response.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 4 — Implementation (July 2023)

records.title: Use a structure, then revisit your diagnosis
records.text:
A problem-solving model should discipline inquiry while allowing new evidence to change the diagnosis.
Define and analyse the problem before choosing a response.
Generate possible solutions, choose an appropriate one and plan action.
Implement the response while monitoring its effectiveness.
Return to earlier steps when new information changes what you understand.
SARA offers another structure: scanning, analysis, response and assessment.
The value of a model is consistent reasoning, not rigidly completing boxes.
Imagine repeated late case reviews are initially described as a motivation problem. During analysis, counterparts show that the review rota conflicts with another duty. The responsible action is to revise the problem definition, not protect the original diagnosis. The lesson presents a six-step process from definition through monitoring, while warning that real problem-solving moves back and forth. It also introduces SARA as an alternative structure. The particular model matters less than using a consistent method to identify, deconstruct and address the issue. Compare possible responses with the people who will implement them, and monitor whether the response changes the problem rather than only completing a task.
Re-entering problem diagnosis when implementation stalls
Define and analyse: Clarify the observed problem and examine evidence, causes and context.
Consider and choose: Develop options and judge which response best fits the problem and constraints.
Plan and implement: Agree practical action with those who must carry it out.
Monitor and revisit: Assess effectiveness and return to definition or analysis if the evidence changes.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 4 — Implementation (July 2023)

records.title: New evidence can change the problem you are solving
records.text:
A consistent method should help you revise a diagnosis, not protect the first explanation.
Separate an observed difficulty from your explanation of its cause.
Seek the perspective of the people affected and consider more than one response.
Monitor the response and return to definition or analysis when it does not address the problem. Resilience includes learning and adaptation.
A response teaches you about the problem when you examine its effects.
Imagine you initially explain late reviews as low motivation. A counterpart then shows that the roster gives the same person two essential duties at once. The new evidence does not settle every question, but it changes the problem you should investigate. A consistent method creates space to revise the diagnosis. Compare a response directed at motivation with one directed at conflicting responsibilities, and decide what observation would help distinguish them. The source describes problem-solving as moving back and forth rather than following a rigid line. The invented example prepares you to hear another group’s perspective in the official activity.
How new operational evidence reshapes the problem definition
Initial signal: Repeated reviews appear late.
Counterpart evidence: The review rota conflicts with an essential duty.
Revised response: Test an agreed scheduling change and examine its effect.
Initial proposal: Late reviews show that staff do not value the new procedure. (This assigns motive from an observed delay.)
More defensible approach: Reviews are late; compare duties, authority, resources and understanding with the staff affected. (This preserves the concern while opening the causal explanation to evidence.)

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 4 — Implementation (July 2023)

records.title: Test your plan from the counterpart’s position
records.text:
The practical activity asks you to work through the consequences of a plan with others, rather than obtain one model answer.
Use the previous planning work as the basis for discussion.
Adopt the perspective of the counterpart or beneficiary affected by another group’s plan.
Identify concerns and explain how they connect to implementation.
Use a recognised problem-solving process to develop responses through dialogue.
Preserve disagreement and uncertainty for facilitated reflection.
The exercise develops perspective-taking and shared problem-solving.
The official activity builds on the plans prepared in Lesson 3. Groups exchange their work and consider how the plan would affect them as counterparts or beneficiaries. They then discuss concerns with the group that prepared the plan and explore possible responses. The workbench provides a place to organise your thinking, but it cannot reproduce the other person’s perspective or a facilitated discussion by itself. If you are studying independently, draft your concerns and the questions you would ask before selecting a response. Treat these as your own analysis, then seek feedback when a facilitator or colleague is available. Self-confirmation records participation, not independently assessed implementation skill.
Examining change friction from the counterpart chair
Review the plan: Understand the activity and intended result before judging its implications.
Change perspective: Explore how a counterpart or beneficiary may experience the proposed implementation.
Discuss and solve: Connect concerns to evidence and use a consistent method to consider responses.
Reflect: Identify what changed in your understanding and what still requires dialogue.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 4 — Implementation (July 2023)

records.title: Ask what changed and why
records.text:
Evaluation supports decisions about progress, shortcomings and future action. It needs a reference in the original plan.
Ask whether the engagement worked, what did not work and why.
Use the planned objectives and performance framework as a reference.
Distinguish delivered activities from evidence about results.
Use evaluation to support learning, improvement, transparency and accountability.
Evaluation is valuable when it informs a defensible decision.
Imagine a project delivered every scheduled workshop, yet the institution is unsure whether the intended practice improved. Evaluation starts from the objective and the evidence needed to judge progress, not from a desire to produce a favourable story. The lesson connects evaluation to planning because a clear plan supplies the reference for the questions being asked. Consider what changed, what did not change and why, while being clear about the limits of the available evidence. Findings should support learning and practical decisions. This invented example does not establish that training succeeded or failed; it shows why a delivery record alone cannot answer the outcome question.
Separating planned activity completion from observable change
Planned objective: Identify the change the programme was intended to achieve.
Evidence of progress: Examine information relevant to that change, not only completed activities.
Interpretation: Explore what worked, what did not and the possible reasons.
Decision: Use the findings to improve practice, inform adjustments and account for results.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 5 — Evaluation & Adjustment (July 2023)

records.title: A favourable comparison is not the whole explanation
records.text:
Two observations may differ because practice changed, because the observation changed, or because other conditions changed.
Check definitions, selection and timing before comparing observations.
Combine relevant quantitative and qualitative evidence; explain limitations and alternative interpretations.
Do not let an overall improvement hide a documented unequal effect. Rights and gender sensitivity belong within evaluation reasoning.
Report the pattern and its limits, including whose experience the pattern conceals.
An invented report says documentation improved after a new routine was introduced. That is worth investigating, but the sequence alone does not establish cause. Perhaps the sample changed, another initiative began or some shifts experienced improvement while others faced new barriers. Ask what the comparison supports and what it leaves uncertain. Qualitative information can help explain patterns, while a clear sampling method helps you judge the numerical evidence. The lesson asks for honest, impartial and rights- and gender-sensitive evaluation. That means reporting relevant limitations and unequal effects even when the headline looks favourable.
Testing alternative explanations behind an apparently positive trend
Observed difference: What does the evidence show, using comparable definitions?
Possible explanations: What intervention and contextual factors may contribute?
Responsible conclusion: State the finding, its limits and implications without overstating causation.
Initial proposal: The figure rose after the initiative, so the initiative worked. (This moves from sequence to a causal claim without examining alternatives.)
More defensible approach: The observed measure improved; examine comparability, other influences and differences between groups before explaining the change. (This retains the observation while making its interpretation accountable.)

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 5 — Evaluation & Adjustment (July 2023)

records.title: Protect credibility and choose appropriate roles
records.text:
Who evaluates, how they work and whose experience is included all affect the credibility of findings.
The 2023 plan names OIOS, DPET, mission evaluation units, Police Division inspections, and SPC or third-party support when called upon.
Clarify the applicable evaluation role and process rather than assuming every actor must evaluate every activity.
Use professional methods and remain honest, self-reflective, impartial and transparent.
Keep human rights and gender sensitivity within the evaluation design.
An evaluator not involved in delivery can help reduce undue influence and bias.
Credibility requires sound methods, appropriate roles and openness to inconvenient evidence.
Imagine an adviser is proud of an activity and is asked to review its results. Familiarity can help explain the context, but it can also shape what the adviser notices or overlooks. The lesson suggests engaging evaluators who were not involved as one way to reduce undue influence and bias. It also names several UN and external evaluation roles. These references describe the July 2023 teaching source; they are not instructions to bypass current mission arrangements. Whatever the arrangement, the work should be professional, honest, impartial and sensitive to human rights and gender. Include relevant experiences instead of allowing the most convenient voices to define the result.
Balancing independence, access, and counterpart participation in roles
Evaluation roles: Clarify mandate, responsibility and available expertise for this evaluation.
Professional method: Use an agreed, appropriate method and disclose limitations.
Impartial judgement: Consider how involvement, expectations or selective evidence could influence findings.
Inclusive perspective: Examine rights and gender implications and whose experience is represented.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 5 — Evaluation & Adjustment (July 2023)

records.title: Design the evaluation before collecting more data
records.text:
Limited resources make a focused evaluation design and clear communication especially important.
Engage those being evaluated and explain the purpose in advance.
Define scope, topics and indicators before selecting data-collection tools.
Choose methods, instruments and sampling that can answer the questions.
Consider quantitative and qualitative analysis, validity and reliability.
Plan the reporting format, audience and involvement of counterparts.
Collect evidence because it answers an evaluation question.
Imagine being asked to evaluate a project with little time and no large evaluation team. Collecting every available document is unlikely to solve the problem. The lesson recommends planning the scope, topics and indicators, then selecting methods, instruments and sampling. Decide what quantitative and qualitative information can answer the questions and what limitations affect its interpretation. Engage the people being evaluated so they understand the purpose and process. Partnerships may help address resource constraints, but roles and communication still need to be clear. Plan how findings will be discussed and used from the beginning; a technically competent report has little value if nobody can act on it.
Matching evaluation questions to defensible evidence sources
Purpose and engagement: Explain the evaluation and involve relevant people from the outset.
Scope and evidence: Link topics and indicators to methods, instruments and sampling.
Analysis quality: Consider validity, reliability and the strengths of qualitative and quantitative information.
Communication and use: Agree how findings will reach stakeholders in a format they can use.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 5 — Evaluation & Adjustment (July 2023)

records.title: Explain your response to recommendations
records.text:
An evaluation recommendation requires an explicit, reasoned response and follow-through.
Accept recommendations fully when justified and take action to implement them.
For partial acceptance, identify which elements are accepted and explain disagreement.
If rejecting a recommendation, state the reasons.
Connect the response to the findings and the changes required in implementation.
Keep a distinction between an evidence-based disagreement and ignoring an unwelcome conclusion.
Accountability includes explaining what you will do with the findings.
Imagine an evaluation recommends changing an activity and its reporting arrangement. The implementation team agrees with the activity change but believes part of the reporting proposal would not answer the evaluation concern. The lesson allows full acceptance, partial acceptance or rejection, but each response carries responsibility. Partial acceptance should identify what is agreed, what is disputed and why. Rejection also requires reasons. An unfavourable finding should not disappear simply because it is uncomfortable. Make the proposed action and the rationale understandable to those who need to follow it. This is a way to turn evaluation into a transparent management decision rather than a report that is merely filed.
Documenting Accept, Partially Accept, or Reject management responses
Fully accept: Agree with the recommendation and take action to implement it.
Partially accept: Specify accepted and disputed elements, with reasons for the disagreement.
Reject with reasons: Explain why the recommendation is not valid or appropriate in this case.
Follow through: Make the resulting implementation response explicit and review its progress.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 5 — Evaluation & Adjustment (July 2023)

records.title: Practise evaluation without borrowing an answer
records.text:
The practical activity applies evaluation to a changed situation and asks you to consider its consequences.
Read the participant situation and relate it to your own planned activities and indicators.
Prepare an evaluation, three to five adjustment recommendations and their implications for the original plan.
Identify what you learned about your earlier decisions.
Present and discuss your reasoning when a facilitated group is available.
Keep the facilitator’s expected-response material outside your independent preparation.
Explain how evidence supports both your recommendation and your reflection.
The official exercise asks participants to evaluate progress in a changed situation, prepare recommendations and examine the effect on the initial plan. Use the participant information and your own earlier objectives rather than trying to reproduce a model response. A recommendation should connect a finding to an action and explain its implications. Reflection then asks what your earlier planning assumed and what you would investigate or handle differently. The workbench can hold that reasoning, but it does not independently establish evaluation competence. If you study alone, prepare your work for later discussion. The scenario-specific expected responses remain facilitator material and are not supplied as feedback here.
Structuring objective variance before using the Module 5 workbench
Read the situation: Distinguish the participant information from assumptions you may be adding.
Evaluate against the plan: Use objectives and relevant indicators to explain the significance of developments.
Recommend and explain: Prepare three to five adjustments and identify implications for the initial plan.
Reflect and discuss: Identify learning and test the reasoning through facilitated or peer discussion.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 5 — Evaluation & Adjustment (July 2023)

records.section: Recognise when and what to transition
records.title: An activity transition is a new responsibility
records.text:
This lesson concerns handing over or closing a specific CBD activity. It does not describe the drawdown of a whole mission.
A transition may hand responsibility to a national counterpart or another CBD actor.
An activity may last longer than one adviser’s deployment.
Closing one engagement can begin a succeeding process.
Distinguish the status of the activity from the departure date of an individual adviser.
Define what is being handed over, to whom and in what continuing context.
Imagine your deployment is ending while an institutional improvement activity is still under way. Your departure does not establish that the objective has been achieved or that the national counterpart is ready to carry every responsibility. The lesson uses transition for a particular CBD activity, not as another term for mission drawdown. A handover may involve a counterpart, another adviser or another actor, depending on the activity and the situation. Begin by identifying the work and responsibilities that will continue. This keeps the discussion focused on continuity and ownership rather than on an administrative date alone. The example is invented and does not describe a CARANA outcome.
Handover as phased continuity rather than sudden departure
Activity: Define the specific work and objective within the broader CBD process.
Continuity: Identify what must continue beyond one person’s deployment.
Successor or counterpart: Clarify the actor who may take responsibility and what they need to do so.
Transition scope: Keep the activity-level decision distinct from overall mission drawdown.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 6 — Transition & Handover (July 2023)

records.section: Recognise when and what to transition
records.title: Use evidence and context to recognise a trigger
records.text:
Transition may follow achieved objectives or a significant change that makes the original activity no longer feasible.
Ideally, evaluation shows enough progress toward the objective to support transition.
Political, security or legal changes may prevent an activity from continuing as planned.
Counterpart decisions and changes in the mission mandate can also trigger a transition process.
Clarify the significance of the trigger rather than treating every change as proof of readiness.
A trigger starts a reasoned decision process; it does not replace assessment.
Imagine an evaluation indicates progress toward an objective at the same time that the operating environment changes. These are different kinds of information, both potentially relevant to transition. The lesson identifies achievement of objectives as an ideal trigger, while recognising that major contextual changes can prevent the original activity from continuing. National counterpart decisions and mandate changes may also matter. Explain what has changed, why it affects the activity and what responsibilities remain. Do not imply that an activity ended because it succeeded when the actual reason is that conditions prevented completion. Honest framing helps stakeholders plan the next step and understand unresolved needs.
Mandate timelines vs readiness and context transition triggers
Progress evidence: Use evaluation to establish whether sufficient progress supports transition.
Contextual change: Examine political, security or legal developments that affect feasibility.
Institutional decision: Consider counterpart and mandate decisions relevant to the activity.
Reasoned assessment: Explain why the trigger matters and what is still required.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 6 — Transition & Handover (July 2023)

records.section: Build ownership and coordinate the decision
records.title: Four principles make transition a process
records.text:
Early planning, UN integration, local ownership and communication should shape transition throughout the activity.
Begin planning early, consider more than one scenario and keep the plan flexible.
Coordinate relevant UN actors from the outset.
Engage counterparts and secure meaningful local leadership and ownership.
Communicate consistently so different stakeholders understand the intended responsibilities and limits.
Transition readiness grows through coordinated preparation, not a final ceremony.
Imagine a handover meeting is scheduled, but the receiving institution has not helped plan it and several partners expect different things to continue. The meeting itself cannot resolve those gaps. The lesson’s four principles ask you to start earlier, coordinate across relevant UN actors, develop local ownership and manage expectations through communication. These principles reinforce one another. Communication without ownership may describe a decision people cannot sustain. Early planning without integration may leave another actor’s obligations unresolved. Ask which principle is least supported in your plan and what evidence would show progress. A useful answer identifies a practical gap rather than simply repeating the four labels.
How the four Lesson 6 principles reinforce sustainable handover
Early planning: Prepare scenarios and remain flexible as the activity develops.
UN integration: Coordinate with relevant UN actors at tactical and operational levels.
Local ownership: Engage local leadership and counterparts in shaping and sustaining responsibility.
Communication: Manage expectations with clear, consistent messages about what will change.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 6 — Transition & Handover (July 2023)

records.section: Build ownership and coordinate the decision
records.title: Distinguish authority from coordination
records.text:
The 2023 lesson plan assigns the initiation decision to the Head of Police Component, informed by the responsible adviser’s advice.
The Head of Police Component decides to initiate transition and assigns responsibilities.
The responsible adviser provides informed advice and coordinates dialogue when assigned.
Involve relevant UN actors and external stakeholders whose responsibilities or interests are affected.
Work toward consensus and manage expectations with sensitivity.
Use current mission authority and arrangements when applying the source in practice.
Advice, decision authority and coordination are related responsibilities, not interchangeable ones.
Imagine you have assembled evidence that an activity could transition. The lesson does not treat that analysis as permission for an adviser to make every decision alone. It assigns the decision to initiate the process to the Head of Police Component, taking the responsible adviser’s advice into account. Assigned transition responsibilities then require proactive dialogue and coordination. Relevant actors may include national law enforcement, civil society, donors and other partners as well as UN entities. This is the arrangement described in the July 2023 plan; real application must follow current mission authority. Make clear who advises, who decides and who will carry the resulting responsibilities.
Deciding accountability vs coordinating partner roles
Advice: The responsible adviser explains evidence, options, needs and implications.
Initiation decision: The Head of Police Component considers advice and assigns transition responsibilities.
Coordination: Assigned actors engage leadership, relevant UN entities and external stakeholders.
Shared expectations: Clarify responsibilities and communicate sensitively while working toward consensus.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 6 — Transition & Handover (July 2023)

records.title: Phase responsibility and test readiness
records.text:
Transition planning should combine performance evidence, integrated assessment and continuing support needs.
Review objectives and performance measures regularly rather than assuming readiness.
Assess rights implications and how transition may affect women, men, girls and boys.
Consider political and security uncertainty, funding and contingency scenarios.
Hand over tasks over time while monitoring progress and counterpart capacity.
Plan continued political and financial support, including gender-responsive resource requirements.
The pace of handover should follow assessed responsibilities and capability.
Imagine a counterpart can lead one part of an activity but still needs support for another. A phased handover can reflect that difference more responsibly than an all-at-once transfer. The lesson connects transition planning to objectives, performance measures and an integrated assessment involving counterparts and relevant UN actors. Human rights and gender analysis belong in that assessment, not as an afterthought. Consider alternative scenarios if political conditions, security or funding change. Monitor the ability to assume residual responsibilities as external involvement reduces. Sustainable support may require continued political commitment and predictable funding, with resources allocated in ways that address women’s needs and priorities.
Staging shared benchmarks before formal transition readiness
Assess readiness: Review progress, responsibilities and counterpart capacity using relevant evidence.
Examine different impacts: Make human rights and gender analysis part of the integrated assessment.
Phase and monitor: Transfer tasks over time and check capability as external engagement reduces.
Sustain and prepare: Address long-term political/resources needs and contingencies for changing conditions.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 6 — Transition & Handover (July 2023)

records.title: Rehearse the conversation behind the handover
records.text:
A counterpart’s agreement should reflect an understood responsibility, not pressure to accept a date.
Name the work and support that would change, then invite the receiving actor’s interpretation.
Explain evidence and uncertainty without promising resources or authority you do not control.
Record unresolved concerns for the appropriate decision and coordination process. Use the official paired exercise for dialogue and reflection when available.
Test understanding of continuing responsibility before treating agreement as readiness.
Imagine a counterpart says they agree to the handover date but later explains that one necessary support function has no continuing resource. It would be easy to treat the first statement as consent and the second as resistance. Instead, ask what responsibility they understood they were accepting. A useful conversation makes the evidence, support and uncertainty visible to both sides. It also recognises the limits of the adviser’s authority. The official exercise uses paired perspectives under an assumption that objectives have been achieved. Our invented conversation adds preparation for that dialogue; it is not a model answer to the exercise.
Walking through critical dialogue steps for handover confirmation
Adviser account: Explain the proposed responsibility and the evidence.
Counterpart account: Ask what can be sustained and what remains difficult.
Joint clarification: Document agreement, uncertainty and the next authorised decision.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 6 — Transition & Handover (July 2023)

records.title: Prepare a transition you can explain to both sides
records.text:
The official practice uses the adviser’s and counterpart’s perspectives to examine a transition process and its challenges.
Work from the participant exercise and its stated assumption about achieved objectives.
Outline a transition process and identify challenges and possible remedies.
Use different perspectives to test responsibilities, expectations and continuity.
Discuss and reflect in a facilitated setting when available.
Keep an independently prepared plan distinct from a validated readiness decision.
A defensible handover explains continuity, ownership and unresolved conditions.
The official exercise asks participants to work in pairs, one as the adviser and the other as the local counterpart. Under its stated assumption that objectives have been achieved, they outline a transition and examine challenges and possible remedies. The pair then returns to discussion and reflection. The workbench supports individual preparation, but it cannot make the counterpart’s judgement or authorise a transition. If working alone, record what you would need to ask the receiving actor, what you expect them to continue and what remains uncertain. Use the plan as a basis for dialogue. The facilitator’s expected response is deliberately not provided in this learner adaptation.
Clarifying mutual obligations for both incoming and outgoing teams
State the exercise assumption: Keep the participant scenario assumptions separate from verified real-world readiness.
Outline the process: Explain responsibilities, sequence and what the receiving actor will continue.
Test both perspectives: Consider challenges and possible remedies through adviser–counterpart dialogue.
Reflect and validate: Record remaining uncertainty and obtain appropriate review before a real transition decision.

source.label: UNPOL Job-Specific Training: CBD Lesson 6 — Transition & Handover (July 2023)

records.title: Conflict analysis and baseline
records.text: Situation analysis is the first step in any CBD process. To improve a specific situation, one must have a clear understanding of the situation in the first place. Proper analysis defines a baseline: evaluating progress and determining whether a goal has been reached require a reference point or state. Multiple forms of analysis examine different dimensions, such as conflict, response and CBD.

records.title: Performance framework
records.text: Evaluation of performance requires objectives that are measurable. Measurability is easiest achieved using performance indicators. A performance framework provides information required for evaluation at a later stage and ties planning to evaluation for future decision-making. Objective setting and PI/KPI setting go hand-in-hand. PIs and KPIs are primary indicators of progress toward an intended result.

records.title: Logframe planning
records.text: CBD advisers are expected to use the Logframe matrix to support planning of CBD activities. A Logframe is a tool used in the Logical Framework Approach, consisting of a matrix that provides an overview of a project goal, activities and anticipated results. It structures project components and activities and relates them to one another. It identifies measures by which anticipated results will be monitored.

records.title: Local policing context
records.text: Local problems require local solutions that account for local organisational culture. Established policing practices cannot simply be imported from outside the host-State into a post-conflict setting. Police reform requires local solutions developed in partnership with stakeholders. Prevailing organisational culture shapes how police officers act and behave and affects the success or failure of CBD.

records.title: Purpose of evaluation
records.text: Evaluation generates information on the progress of programmes and projects that allows advisers and relevant stakeholders to make decisions and adjust plans where needed. It supports improvement, knowledge generation, transparency and accountability. Evaluation is the counterpart to planning and requires a plan as a reference. Evaluators not involved in the programme can help avoid undue influence and bias.

records.title: Triggers for transition
records.text: Transition takes place upon achieving the objective or in reaction to significant environmental changes that prevent completion. It can respond to changes in the area and dimension addressed or the country situation, such as political, security or legal change. National counterpart decisions and changes in the Mission Mandate can also trigger transition. Ideally evaluation recognises that sufficient progress toward the objective has been made.
